title: 💰 Decimal Market
description: Welcome to the Decimal Market — the busiest bazaar in town! You have just been hired as the youngest shopkeeper in the market. Every transaction involves decimals, percentages, and money calculations. From pricing products to calculating discounts, from managing stock to counting profits — can you master decimals and become the Market Champion?
subject: mathematics
how_to_play: You run a shop in a busy market for 14 days — every transaction involves decimals!
Each round presents a market challenge where you must use decimals and percentages to make decisions.
Watch your dashboard — your Shop Sections, Supplies, and Customer Trust are interconnected.
NPCs like Shopkeeper Meera (mentor), Supplier Suresh, Bargain-Hunter Bina, and Apprentice Arjun react to your choices.
Random events like festival rushes and surprise inspections will test your decimal skills.
Keep your Calculation Accuracy high — wrong decimals mean lost money and angry customers!
learning_objectives: Understand decimal place value — tenths, hundredths, thousandths
Add and subtract decimals with precision
Convert between fractions, decimals, and percentages
Apply decimal skills to real-world money problems
cultural_context: Indian bazaar/market setting connecting decimals to real-world money handling, rupee calculations, and everyday commerce familiar to students

behaviors.message: Your decimal basics need strengthening! Remember, the decimal point separates whole numbers from parts. In 12.75, the 7 is in the tenths place (7/10) and the 5 is in the hundredths place (5/100). Every position has a value!
Too many billing errors! A customer paid ₹15.50 for a ₹15.05 item — you mixed up the digits! In decimals, 15.50 and 15.05 are very different. The position of each digit matters enormously!
Your decimal calculations are becoming sharp! I watched you add ₹25.75 + ₹13.48 in your head and get ₹39.23 — perfect! Customers notice when the bill is always correct.
You are a decimal wizard! Your mental maths is faster than the calculator. I have been in this market for 20 years and even I cannot compute percentage discounts as quickly as you!
You underpaid me by ₹3.25 on the last order! The invoice said ₹875.50 but you only gave ₹872.25. In the wholesale business, every decimal counts. Please double-check your payments!
It is a pleasure doing business with you! Your payments are always exact — right down to the last paisa. I will give you priority on my best stock from now on!
You are my best customer in the entire market! Your decimal accuracy is legendary. I am giving you a permanent 5% discount — because doing business with you is a joy!
You charged me ₹99.99 but the price tag says ₹89.99! That is ₹10 too much! I know my decimals — do not try to overcharge me. I want my money back immediately!
You calculated my 15% discount in your head — ₹250 minus 15% equals ₹212.50! That was faster than my phone calculator! I trust this shop. I am telling all my friends to come here!

I have told the entire neighbourhood — this is the ONLY shop where the bill is always right! Not one paisa wrong. In a market full of errors, your decimal precision makes you the most trusted shopkeeper around!
I am confused — is 0.5 bigger or smaller than 0.50? They look different but Meera says they are the same! And why is 0.3 less than 0.30... wait, or are they equal too? Decimals are confusing!
I gave a customer change of ₹3.5 instead of ₹3.50 and they stared at me. Then I accidentally wrote ₹1250 on a ₹12.50 price tag — no decimal point! Everyone is frustrated with my mistakes...

I finally get it! The decimal point is like a wall — the left side is whole numbers and the right side is parts. Tenths, hundredths, thousandths! And 0.5 equals 0.50 because trailing zeros do not change value. You are a great teacher!

I just calculated a customer's total all by myself! ₹45.75 + ₹23.50 + ₹8.25 = ₹77.50! I lined up the decimal points and added column by column. Thank you for teaching me — I want to run my own shop someday!

rounds.situation: It is your first day at the Decimal Market! Shopkeeper Meera shows you around. Your very first customer wants to buy a notebook priced at ₹12.50. She hands you a ₹20 note. 'How much change do I give back?' you wonder. ₹20.00 minus ₹12.50 — this is where your decimal journey begins!
rounds.goal: Understand what decimals are and how they represent money values.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: A decimal number has a whole number part and a fractional part, separated by a decimal point. In ₹12.50, the '12' is the whole rupees and '.50' means 50 paise (half a rupee). The decimal point is the bridge between wholes and parts.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do we use decimals instead of fractions when dealing with money? What makes decimals easier for everyday transactions?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon Indian market shop on opening day, young shopkeeper behind colorful counter with products, Shopkeeper Meera pointing at a price tag showing ₹12.50, warm welcoming bazaar atmosphere, Pixar-style

choices.label: A. In 3.472, the digit 7 is in the hundredths place and its value is 0.07
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ In 3.472: 3 = ones, 4 = tenths (0.4), 7 = hundredths (0.07), 2 = thousandths (0.002). Each place is 10× smaller as you move right: ones → tenths → hundredths → thousandths. The 7 in the hundredths place means 7/100 = 0.07.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. In 3.472, the digit 7 is in the tenths place and its value is 0.7
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 The 4 is in the tenths place (first after decimal), not the 7. Count from the decimal point: 4 (tenths), 7 (hundredths), 2 (thousandths). So 7 is in the HUNDREDTHS place with a value of 0.07, not 0.7.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.label: C. In 3.472, the digit 7 is in the thousandths place and its value is 0.007
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 The 2 (last digit) is in the thousandths place, not the 7. Reading 3.472: 3 ones, 4 tenths, 7 hundredths, 2 thousandths. The 7 is in the HUNDREDTHS place (second after decimal) with a value of 0.07.

skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: D. In 3.472, the digit 7 has a value of 70 because 7 is always 70 in a number
choices.learning_concept: Place Value Changes a Digit's Worth
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 A digit's value depends on its POSITION! 7 in the tens place = 70, but 7 in the hundredths place = 0.07. In 3.472, the 7 is after the decimal point in the hundredths position, so its value is 7/100 = 0.07. Position matters!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

rounds.situation: Arjun made a terrible mistake! He wrote ₹1250 on a price tag instead of ₹12.50. A customer tried to return an item saying 'I am NOT paying twelve hundred and fifty rupees for a pen!' You need to explain to Arjun WHY the position of the decimal point matters so much.
rounds.goal: Understand decimal place value — how the position of each digit determines its value.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: In the decimal number 12.50: the '1' is in the tens place (value = 10), the '2' is in the ones place (value = 2), the '5' is in the tenths place (value = 0.5), and the '0' is in the hundredths place (value = 0). Moving the decimal point changes EVERYTHING!
rounds.reflection_prompt: What is the difference between 1.5, 15, 150, and 0.15? How does the position of the decimal point change the meaning?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon market shop with a shocked customer holding a price tag reading ₹1250, embarrassed young helper (Arjun) realizing mistake should be ₹12.50, Shopkeeper Meera explaining with a place value chart on the wall, Pixar-style

choices.label: A. 0.35 > 0.305 because in the hundredths place, 5 > 0
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Compare decimals place by place from left to right. Both have 0 ones and 3 tenths. In the hundredths place: 0.35 has 5, but 0.305 has 0. Since 5 > 0, we get 0.35 > 0.305. Tip: you can write 0.35 as 0.350 to make comparison easier — adding trailing zeros doesn't change the value!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. 0.305 > 0.35 because 305 is bigger than 35
choices.learning_concept: Decimal Comparison — Not Whole Number Comparison
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You can't ignore the decimal point and compare like whole numbers! 305 > 35 is true for whole numbers, but 0.305 < 0.35. Write them with equal decimal places: 0.350 vs 0.305. Now compare: 350 thousandths > 305 thousandths. So 0.35 > 0.305.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: C. 0.35 = 0.305 because they both start with 0.3
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Starting with the same digits doesn't make them equal — you must check ALL places! 0.35 = 0.350 and 0.305 differ in the hundredths place: 5 vs 0. So 0.350 > 0.305. Always compare every decimal place from left to right.

skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

choices.label: D. 0.305 > 0.35 because 0.305 has more digits after the decimal
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 More decimal digits does NOT mean a bigger number! 0.35 has 2 decimal digits but is LARGER than 0.305 (3 decimal digits). To compare: pad with zeros → 0.350 vs 0.305. Then 350 > 305, so 0.35 > 0.305.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

rounds.situation: Three suppliers offer you the same product at different prices: Supplier A offers it at ₹8.45, Supplier B at ₹8.54, and Supplier C at ₹8.5. Which is the cheapest? Which is the most expensive? Arjun says: '₹8.5 must be cheapest because it has fewer digits.' Is he right?
rounds.goal: Compare and order decimals correctly by looking at place value, not number of digits.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: To compare decimals, first make them all the same length by adding trailing zeros: ₹8.45, ₹8.54, ₹8.50. Now compare digit by digit from left to right. The ones digits are all 8. The tenths: 4, 5, 5. Since 4 < 5, ₹8.45 is the cheapest. Then compare hundredths of the two 8.5_ numbers: 4 < 0, wait — no! 8.54 > 8.50.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Arjun thought 8.5 was less than 8.45 because it has fewer digits. Why is this wrong? What is the correct way to compare decimals?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon market scene with three supplier stalls showing price tags ₹8.45, ₹8.54, and ₹8.5, young shopkeeper with magnifying glass comparing prices, thought bubble showing comparison, Pixar-style

choices.label: A. 4.56 + 2.8 = 7.36 (line up decimal points: 4.56 + 2.80 = 7.36)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ When adding decimals, LINE UP THE DECIMAL POINTS! Write 2.8 as 2.80 to match decimal places. Then add column by column from right: 6+0=6, 5+8=13 (write 3, carry 1), 4+2+1=7. Answer: 7.36. The decimal point stays aligned throughout!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. 4.56 + 2.8 = 7.44 (56 + 28 = 84... wait, that's 7.84... I mean 7.44)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 The error comes from not aligning decimal points properly. Write 2.8 as 2.80 (add a trailing zero). Now line up: 4.56 + 2.80. Add: 6+0=6, 5+8=13 (write 3, carry 1), 4+2+1=7. Answer: 7.36. Always align those decimal points!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

choices.label: C. 4.56 + 2.8 = 6.64 (I forgot to carry the 1)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 When digits add to 10 or more, you must carry! 5 tenths + 8 tenths = 13 tenths. Write 3 in tenths, carry 1 to ones. Then 4 + 2 + 1(carried) = 7. So 4.56 + 2.80 = 7.36, not 6.64. Always check your carrying!

skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

choices.label: D. 4.56 + 2.8 = 4.84 (just add 56 + 28 = 84, so 4.84)
choices.learning_concept: Add Whole and Decimal Parts Together
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You added only the decimal parts and kept only one whole number. You must add the whole number parts too: 4 + 2 = 6, plus any carry from the decimal part. Correct: 4.56 + 2.80 = 7.36. Line up decimal points and add ALL digits.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

rounds.situation: A customer buys five items: ₹25.75, ₹13.48, ₹8.25, ₹42.60, and ₹6.92. They want one combined bill. Can you add all five decimal numbers correctly? Remember — the decimal points must line up perfectly, or the total will be wrong!
rounds.goal: Add decimal numbers by lining up decimal points and adding column by column.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: When adding decimals, the golden rule is: LINE UP THE DECIMAL POINTS. Write each number so that ones are under ones, tenths under tenths, hundredths under hundredths. Then add each column from right to left, carrying over when needed. The decimal point in the answer goes directly below the others.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why is it so important to line up decimal points when adding? What happens if you accidentally shift one number by one place?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon market shop billing counter, young shopkeeper writing five prices in a column with decimal points perfectly aligned, customer watching, neat handwriting on receipt paper, Pixar-style

choices.label: A. 8.3 − 4.57 = 3.73 (rewrite as 8.30 − 4.57, borrow as needed)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Write 8.3 as 8.30 (add trailing zero). Line up decimal points: 8.30 − 4.57. From right: 0−7 (borrow: 10−7=3), 2−5 (borrow: 12−5=7), 7−4=3. Answer: 3.73. Adding trailing zeros makes subtraction with different decimal lengths much easier!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: B. 8.3 − 4.57 = 4.27 (I subtracted 57 from 83 getting 26... wait, no, 4.27)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Misaligning decimal places causes errors. Write as 8.30 − 4.57 (not 83 − 57). Then subtract column by column with borrowing: hundredths: 10−7=3, tenths: 2−5→borrow→12−5=7, ones: 7−4=3. Answer: 3.73.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

choices.label: C. 8.3 − 4.57 = 3.87 (I made an error borrowing in the tenths place)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Let's trace the borrowing carefully. 8.30 − 4.57: hundredths: 0−7, borrow → 10−7=3. Tenths: now 2 (was 3, gave 1) minus 5, borrow → 12−5=7. Ones: 7 (was 8, gave 1) minus 4 = 3. Answer: 3.73. Double-check each borrow!

skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.

choices.label: D. 8.3 − 4.57 = 3.33 (8−4=4... no, 8−4=3.33... I'm confused)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Don't try to do it in your head — write it out! Step 1: 8.30 − 4.57. Step 2: Start from the RIGHT. Hundredths: 0−7→borrow→10−7=3. Tenths: 2−5→borrow→12−5=7. Ones: 7−4=3. Answer: 3.73. Being systematic prevents errors!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

rounds.situation: A customer bought ₹156.80 worth of goods but wants to return an item worth ₹23.45. She also has a store credit of ₹12.75. You need to calculate: ₹156.80 - ₹23.45 - ₹12.75 = ? Decimal subtraction with borrowing — can you handle it?
rounds.goal: Subtract decimals accurately, including multi-step subtraction with borrowing.
rounds.coaching_moment: Adaptability: Decimal subtraction follows the same rules as whole number subtraction — but you MUST align decimal points first. When a digit on top is smaller than the digit below, borrow from the next column left. ₹156.80 - ₹23.45: hundredths: 0-5 needs borrowing. Take from the 8 tenths...
rounds.reflection_prompt: When subtracting 0 - 5 in the hundredths place, you need to borrow. Where do you borrow from, and how does the borrowing work with decimal places?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon market shop returns counter, customer handing back an item, young shopkeeper carefully writing subtraction on receipt paper, decimal points aligned, borrowed numbers visible, Pixar-style

choices.label: A. 3.45 × 6 = 20.70 (multiply 345 × 6 = 2070, then place decimal: 20.70)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ To multiply a decimal by a whole number: (1) Ignore the decimal point and multiply: 345 × 6 = 2070. (2) Count decimal places in the original (3.45 has 2). (3) Place the decimal 2 places from the right: 20.70 (or 20.7). The total decimal places in the answer equals the decimal places in the factors!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. 3.45 × 6 = 207.0 (345 × 6 = 2070, put decimal after first digit)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You got 2070 right but placed the decimal wrong. 3.45 has 2 decimal places, so place the decimal 2 places from the RIGHT in your answer: 2070 → 20.70. Not 1 place (207.0). A quick estimate confirms: 3.45 × 6 ≈ 3.5 × 6 = 21, so 20.70 makes sense!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: C. 3.45 × 6 = 18.270 (3×6=18, 45×6=270, so 18.270)
choices.learning_concept: Multiply the Entire Number Not Parts
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You can't split a decimal and multiply parts separately like that. Multiply as one number: 345 × 6 = 2070. Then count 2 decimal places from the right: 20.70. Or do it the long way: 3 × 6 = 18, 0.4 × 6 = 2.4, 0.05 × 6 = 0.3 → 18 + 2.4 + 0.3 = 20.7.

skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

choices.label: D. 3.45 × 6 = 3.270 (just multiply 45 × 6 = 270, keep the 3)
choices.learning_concept: Multiply ALL Digits by the Factor
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You must multiply the ENTIRE number by 6, not just the decimal part. 3.45 × 6: the whole number part (3) also gets multiplied! 345 × 6 = 2070 → 20.70. Quick check: 3 × 6 alone is 18, so the answer must be at least 18!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

rounds.situation: Supplier Suresh offers a deal: buy 10 pens at ₹8.75 each, or 100 pens at ₹7.25 each. You need to calculate 10 × ₹8.75 and 100 × ₹7.25 quickly. Meera says there is a shortcut for multiplying by 10 and 100 — do you know it?
rounds.goal: Master the shortcut for multiplying decimals by 10, 100, and 1000 — move the decimal point!
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: When you multiply by 10, move the decimal point one place RIGHT. When you multiply by 100, move it TWO places right. 10 × ₹8.75 = ₹87.50 (decimal moves one place right). 100 × ₹7.25 = ₹725.00 (decimal moves two places right). The shortcut works because our number system is base-10!
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why does moving the decimal point right multiply a number by 10? What happens if you move it LEFT instead?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon market wholesale counter, young shopkeeper with boxes of pens stacked up, price tags showing ₹8.75 and ₹7.25, calculator showing multiplication, decimal point jumping animation arrows, Pixar-style

choices.label: A. 0.4 × 0.3 = 0.12 (4 × 3 = 12, then 2 decimal places → 0.12)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Multiply decimals: (1) Ignore decimals and multiply: 4 × 3 = 12. (2) Count TOTAL decimal places: 0.4 has 1, 0.3 has 1, total = 2. (3) Place decimal 2 from right: 0.12. This makes sense: 0.4 × 0.3 means '4 tenths of 3 tenths' = 12 hundredths = 0.12.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. 0.4 × 0.3 = 1.2 (4 × 3 = 12, put decimal after first digit)
choices.learning_concept: Count ALL Decimal Places in Both Factors
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You only counted 1 decimal place, but there are 2 total (1 from each factor). 4 × 3 = 12, then place decimal 2 places from right → 0.12 (not 1.2). Also, common sense check: 0.4 × 0.3 must be LESS than both 0.4 and 0.3, and 1.2 is bigger than both!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.label: C. 0.4 × 0.3 = 0.7 (add them: 0.4 + 0.3 = 0.7)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 That's the answer to 0.4 + 0.3, not 0.4 × 0.3! Multiplication and addition are different operations. 0.4 × 0.3: multiply 4 × 3 = 12, count 2 decimal places → 0.12. Notice: multiplying two decimals less than 1 gives a SMALLER result.

skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: D. 0.4 × 0.3 = 0.012 (4 × 3 = 12, then 3 decimal places)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You counted 3 decimal places, but there are only 2! 0.4 has 1 decimal place + 0.3 has 1 decimal place = 2 total. So 12 → 0.12 (move decimal 2 places left). Be careful to count only the actual decimal digits in each factor.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

rounds.situation: CRISIS! The electronic cash register just died! It is the busiest hour of the busiest day, and customers are lined up to the door. You have NO calculator, NO machine — just a pen, paper, and your brain. Every bill must be calculated in decimals by hand. Arjun is panicking. Meera is serving from memory. Can you handle the pressure?
rounds.goal: Apply all decimal arithmetic skills under extreme pressure — addition, subtraction, and multiplication without a calculator!
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: When technology fails, your mathematical skills are your backup. If you truly UNDERSTAND decimals — not just push calculator buttons — you can handle any situation. Deep knowledge beats dependence on machines.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Many shopkeepers in India calculate without machines every day. Why does understanding the maths yourself — instead of depending on a calculator — make you a better problem-solver?
rounds.image_prompt: Chaotic cartoon Indian market shop with broken cash register showing error screen, long queue of customers, young shopkeeper calculating on paper with pen, sweat drops, intense concentration, Pixar-style dramatic scene

choices.label: A. 9.36 ÷ 4 = 2.34 (divide normally, keep decimal point aligned)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Divide just like whole numbers, but keep the decimal point straight above in the answer. 9.36 ÷ 4: 9÷4=2 remainder 1, bring down 3→13÷4=3 remainder 1, bring down 6→16÷4=4. Answer: 2.34. The decimal in the answer lines up with the decimal in the dividend!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.
skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

choices.label: B. 9.36 ÷ 4 = 23.4 (936 ÷ 4 = 234, put decimal after first digit)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 The decimal point must stay in the SAME position! 9.36 has the decimal between 9 and 3, so the answer's decimal stays there too: 2.34 (not 23.4). Quick check: 9.36 ÷ 4 should be about 9 ÷ 4 ≈ 2.something, not 23.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: C. 9.36 ÷ 4 = 2.24 (I made an error in the division steps)
choices.learning_concept: Long Division with Decimals — Careful Steps
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Let's trace it carefully: 9÷4=2 remainder 1. Bring 3 down: 13÷4=3 remainder 1 (not 2!). Bring 6 down: 16÷4=4. Answer: 2.34. The middle step: 13÷4=3 (since 4×3=12), not 2. Always check: 4×2.34 = 9.36 ✓.

skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

choices.label: D. 9.36 ÷ 4 = 2.09 (I forgot to bring down digits properly)
choices.learning_concept: Bringing Down Digits in Long Division
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You need to bring down each digit carefully. 9÷4=2 R1, bring down 3→13÷4=3 R1, bring down 6→16÷4=4. Answer: 2.34. Verify: 2.34 × 4 = 9.36 ✓. Always multiply back to check your division!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

rounds.situation: It is sale season! Meera announces: 'All items 20% off!' A customer picks up an item costing ₹450. She asks: 'What is 20% of ₹450? And what is the sale price?' You need to calculate percentages — the bridge between fractions and decimals!
rounds.goal: Understand percentages as 'per hundred' and calculate percentage discounts.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Percent means 'per hundred.' 20% means 20 out of every 100. To find 20% of ₹450: convert 20% to a decimal (0.20), then multiply: 0.20 × 450 = ₹90 discount. Sale price = ₹450 - ₹90 = ₹360. Or use the shortcut: 10% of 450 = 45, so 20% = 45 × 2 = 90.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why is 50% the same as 1/2 and 0.5? Can you express 25%, 75%, and 10% as both fractions and decimals?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon market shop with big SALE banners showing 20% OFF, young shopkeeper calculating discount on a price tag, customer waiting eagerly, bright festive sale atmosphere with colorful bunting, Pixar-style

challenge.question: An item costs ₹450. If the discount is 20%, what is the sale price?
challenge.formula_hint: Discount = price × percentage ÷ 100. Sale price = price − discount.

choices.label: A. 6.847 rounded to 1 decimal place = 6.8 (look at hundredths digit 4: less than 5, round down)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ To round to 1 decimal place (tenths): look at the digit in the NEXT place (hundredths). In 6.847, the tenths digit is 8 and the hundredths digit is 4. Since 4 < 5, round DOWN (keep 8). Answer: 6.8. Rule: 0-4 = round down, 5-9 = round up.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. 6.847 rounded to 1 decimal place = 6.9 (the 4 and 7 together make it round up)
choices.learning_concept: Only Look at the NEXT Digit When Rounding
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 When rounding, only look at the ONE digit IMMEDIATELY after your rounding position. To round to 1 decimal place, look at the hundredths (4). Since 4 < 5, round DOWN to 6.8. Don't look at the 7 — only the NEXT digit matters!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

choices.label: C. 6.847 rounded to 1 decimal place = 7.0 (round the 8 up to 9... no, to 7.0)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You rounded too aggressively! 6.847 to 1 decimal place: the hundredths digit is 4 (< 5), so the tenths digit 8 stays the same → 6.8. You'd only get 7.0 if rounding to the nearest whole number (8 in tenths ≥ 5, so ones rounds up: 7). But we wanted 1 decimal place.

skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.

choices.label: D. 6.847 rounded to 1 decimal place = 6.847 (it's already rounded)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 6.847 has 3 decimal places (tenths, hundredths, thousandths). Rounding to 1 decimal place means keeping only the tenths digit. Look at hundredths (4): since 4 < 5, keep 8 → answer is 6.8. Rounding shortens the number!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

rounds.situation: A customer says: 'I want 3/4 of a kilogram of rice.' Your digital scale shows decimals, not fractions. Another customer says: 'Give me 0.6 kg of dal.' A third asks for '60% of a kilo of sugar.' These are ALL the same type of number — just written differently! Can you convert between fractions, decimals, and percentages?
rounds.goal: Convert fluently between fractions, decimals, and percentages.
rounds.coaching_moment: Adaptability: Fractions, decimals, and percentages are THREE ways to write the SAME number. 3/4 = 0.75 = 75%. To convert: fraction → decimal: divide top by bottom (3÷4=0.75). Decimal → percentage: multiply by 100 (0.75×100=75%). Percentage → fraction: put over 100 and simplify (75/100=3/4).
rounds.reflection_prompt: Can you express 1/3 as a decimal? What happens? Why do some fractions create repeating decimals?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon market grain shop with three customers, digital scale showing decimal weight, conversion chart on wall showing fraction=decimal=percentage, bags of rice and dal, young shopkeeper with balance scale, Pixar-style

choices.label: A. 3/8 = 0.375 (divide 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ To convert a fraction to a decimal, divide the numerator by the denominator. 3 ÷ 8: 3.000 ÷ 8 = 0.375. Check: 0.375 × 8 = 3 ✓. Common conversions to memorize: 1/8=0.125, 1/4=0.25, 3/8=0.375, 1/2=0.5, 5/8=0.625, 3/4=0.75.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: B. 3/8 = 0.38 (put 3 and 8 after the decimal point)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You can't just stick the digits together! Convert by dividing: 3 ÷ 8. Set up long division: 8 goes into 30 three times (24), remainder 6. 8 into 60 seven times (56), remainder 4. 8 into 40 five times (40). Answer: 0.375.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

choices.label: C. 3/8 = 2.666... (divide 8 ÷ 3 = 2.667)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You divided the wrong way! For 3/8, divide 3 BY 8 (numerator ÷ denominator), not 8 by 3. 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375. Remember: the fraction bar means 'divided by' — top ÷ bottom. A proper fraction always gives a decimal less than 1.

skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

choices.label: D. 3/8 = 0.3 (since the numerator is 3, decimal is 0.3)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 0.3 = 3/10, not 3/8. The denominator matters! 3/8 means 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375. Different denominators give different decimals: 3/10 = 0.3, 3/8 = 0.375, 3/5 = 0.6. You must do the actual division.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

challenge.question: A shirt costs ₹249.50. You pay with ₹300. How much change?

rounds.situation: A new government rule says all prices must be rounded to the nearest ₹0.50 (no paise smaller than 50). Your item prices include ₹34.73, ₹89.25, ₹12.48, and ₹56.76. Should ₹34.73 round to ₹34.50 or ₹35.00? What about ₹89.25 — does it stay or change? Rounding rules can get tricky!
rounds.goal: Round decimals to specified places using correct rounding rules (5 or above rounds up, below 5 rounds down).
rounds.coaching_moment: Adaptability: To round to the nearest 0.50, look at the paise after the 50-mark. ₹34.73 is between ₹34.50 and ₹35.00 — since 73 is closer to 50+50=100 than to 50, it rounds UP to ₹35.00. ₹34.23 would round DOWN to ₹34.00 because 23 is closer to 00 than 50. The key digit determines the direction!
rounds.reflection_prompt: When is rounding helpful and when can it be misleading? If a shop always rounds UP, is that fair to customers?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon market shop with government rounding rule poster on wall, young shopkeeper with price tags and a number line showing rounding boundaries, red arrows pointing up or down at each price, Pixar-style

choices.label: A. 0.75 = 75/100 = 3/4 (75 hundredths, simplified by dividing both by 25)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ To convert a decimal to a fraction: (1) Read the place value: 0.75 = 75 hundredths = 75/100. (2) Simplify by finding GCF: GCF(75,100) = 25. (3) Divide both: 75÷25 = 3, 100÷25 = 4. So 0.75 = 3/4. Quick tip: 0.25 = 1/4, 0.5 = 1/2, 0.75 = 3/4.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. 0.75 = 7/5 (put 7 over 5)
choices.learning_concept: Decimals to Fractions — Use Place Value
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You can't just separate the digits! 0.75 means 75 HUNDREDTHS, so the fraction is 75/100. The denominator comes from the place value (2 decimal places = 100). Simplify: 75/100 = 3/4. Note: 7/5 = 1.4, which is way more than 0.75!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: C. 0.75 = 75/10 (put 75 over 10 because there's 1 decimal point)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Count the decimal PLACES, not the decimal point. 0.75 has 2 decimal places (tenths and hundredths), so the denominator is 100 (not 10). 0.75 = 75/100 = 3/4. Rule: 1 place → /10, 2 places → /100, 3 places → /1000.

skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: D. 0.75 = 75/100 and that's the simplest form
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 75/100 IS correct as a fraction, but it's NOT in simplest form! Both 75 and 100 are divisible by 25: 75÷25 = 3, 100÷25 = 4. So 0.75 = 75/100 = 3/4. Always simplify your fractions by dividing by the GCF!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

rounds.situation: Today is complex! A customer buys 3 items at ₹45.75 each and 2 items at ₹32.60 each. She has a ₹50 gift card. She pays the rest in cash with a ₹200 note. How much change does she get? This requires multiplication, addition, and subtraction — all with decimals!
rounds.goal: Solve multi-step money problems combining addition, subtraction, and multiplication of decimals.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Break complex problems into steps. Step 1: 3 × ₹45.75 = ₹137.25. Step 2: 2 × ₹32.60 = ₹65.20. Step 3: Total = ₹137.25 + ₹65.20 = ₹202.45. Step 4: Subtract gift card: ₹202.45 - ₹50.00 = ₹152.45. Step 5: Change from ₹200: ₹200.00 - ₹152.45 = ₹47.55.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why is it important to write down each step instead of trying to do everything in your head at once?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon market shop with a complex bill showing multiple calculations, young shopkeeper writing steps on paper, customer with shopping bags and gift card, cash register and notes visible, Pixar-style

challenge.question: A customer buys 3 items at ₹45.75 each and 2 items at ₹32.60 each. What is the total bill?

choices.label: A. 45% = 0.45 (divide by 100: move decimal point 2 places left)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Percent means 'per hundred' or 'out of 100.' To convert % to decimal, divide by 100 (move decimal 2 places left). 45% = 45 ÷ 100 = 0.45. To go back: 0.45 × 100 = 45%. Other examples: 7% = 0.07, 120% = 1.20, 50% = 0.50.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. 45% = 4.5 (move decimal only 1 place left)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You moved the decimal only 1 place left instead of 2. 'Per cent' = per HUNDRED = ÷ 100. Dividing by 100 moves the decimal 2 places left: 45% → 45. → 4.5 → 0.45. Common sense: 45% is less than half, so it must be less than 0.5. 4.5 is way too big!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.label: C. 45% = 0.045 (move decimal 3 places left)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You moved the decimal 3 places instead of 2. Percent = per HUNDRED (not per thousand), so divide by 100 (move 2 places left). 45% = 45 ÷ 100 = 0.45. Moving 3 places would be dividing by 1000, giving a number that's way too small.

skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

choices.label: D. 45% = 45.0 (percent just means the number stays the same as a decimal)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 45% does NOT equal 45! The % symbol means 'divided by 100.' So 45% = 45/100 = 0.45. Think of it this way: 100% = 1 (the whole), so 45% must be less than 1. 45% of something is less than half.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

widget_answer.prompt: A product costs 125.00 with 25% markup. What's the selling price?

rounds.situation: CRISIS! The tax auditor arrives unannounced! He wants to see your full stock records — purchase prices, selling prices, quantities, and profit margins for every item. But your records are a mess of mixed formats: some prices in fractions ('bought at 3/4 of MRP'), some in percentages ('sold at 15% markup'), some in decimals. Nothing matches! You have 2 hours to reconcile everything before the auditor returns!
rounds.goal: Apply ALL decimal skills — place value, arithmetic, conversions, rounding, and percentages — in a high-pressure audit situation.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Real-world math rarely comes in neat textbook format. You will see fractions, decimals, percentages, and whole numbers mixed together. The ability to convert between formats and verify calculations is what separates a reliable professional from an error-prone one.
rounds.reflection_prompt: When different people use different number formats (fractions, decimals, percentages), what problems can arise? How does standardization help?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon tax auditor with magnifying glass at a messy market shop counter, piles of receipts and ledgers, young shopkeeper frantically organizing papers, clock on wall showing time pressure, dramatic tension, Pixar-style

choices.label: A. ₹45.75 + ₹18.50 + ₹6.25 = ₹70.50 (line up decimals and add)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Line up decimal points and add: 45.75 + 18.50 + 6.25. Paise: 5+0+5=10 (write 0, carry 1). Tenths: 7+5+2+1=15 (write 5, carry 1). Ones: 5+8+6+1=20 (write 0, carry 2). Tens: 4+1+2=7. Total: ₹70.50. Money always has 2 decimal places!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Investing effort now for later payoff builds discipline.

choices.label: B. ₹45.75 + ₹18.50 + ₹6.25 = ₹69.50 (I forgot to carry from the paise column)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Check the carrying! Hundredths: 5+0+5=10 paise → write 0, carry 1. Tenths: 7+5+2+1(carry)=15 → write 5, carry 1. Ones: 5+8+6+1(carry)=20 → write 0, carry 2. Tens: 4+1+0+2=7. Answer: ₹70.50. Don't lose track of carries!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: C. ₹45.75 + ₹18.50 + ₹6.25 = ₹70.150 (75+50+25 = 150)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You can't add the decimal parts as whole numbers (75+50+25=150) and stick them after the decimal. You must add column by column: 75+50+25 = 150 paise = ₹1.50. So the decimal part contributes ₹1.50, and the whole part is 45+18+6 = 69. Total: 69 + 1.50 = ₹70.50.

skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

choices.label: D. ₹45.75 + ₹18.50 + ₹6.25 = ₹60.50 (I miscounted the ones column)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Let's recount: after the decimal carries, the ones column has 5+8+6+1(carry) = 20, not 10. Write 0, carry 2 to the tens. Tens: 4+1+0+2 = 7. So the answer is ₹70.50. Always double-check your column totals, especially with carries!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

challenge.question: What is 15% of 80? (Express as a decimal)

rounds.situation: It is time to see if your shop is making money! You bought an item for ₹350.00 (cost price) and sold it for ₹420.50 (selling price). What is your profit? What is the profit percentage? Another item cost ₹200.00 but you had to sell at ₹175.50 because of a sale. What is the loss and loss percentage?
rounds.goal: Calculate profit, loss, and profit/loss percentage using decimal arithmetic.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Profit = Selling Price - Cost Price (when SP > CP). Loss = Cost Price - Selling Price (when CP > SP). Profit % = (Profit ÷ Cost Price) × 100. For your item: Profit = ₹420.50 - ₹350.00 = ₹70.50. Profit% = (70.50 ÷ 350) × 100 = 20.14%. Every shopkeeper must know these formulas!
rounds.reflection_prompt: A shop sells 100 items at 5% profit each. Another sells 10 items at 50% profit each. Which strategy is better in the long run? Why?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon market shop accountant's desk with ledger book showing green profit arrows and red loss arrows, young shopkeeper with calculator comparing two columns, coins and notes stacked, Pixar-style

choices.label: A. Profit = ₹245.50 − ₹178.75 = ₹66.75 (subtract cost from selling price)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Profit = Selling Price − Cost Price. ₹245.50 − ₹178.75: Line up decimals. Hundredths: 0−5 (borrow) → 10−5=5. Tenths: 4−7 (borrow) → 14−7=7. Ones: 4−8 (borrow) → 14−8=6. Tens: 3−7 (borrow) → 13−7=6. Hundreds: 1−1=0. Profit = ₹66.75!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. Profit = ₹245.50 − ₹178.75 = ₹67.75 (I got confused with borrowing)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Close, but the borrowing went wrong somewhere. Let's be careful: 245.50 − 178.75. Hundredths: 10−5=5. Tenths: 14−7=7 (we borrowed). Ones: 14−8=6 (we borrowed from 4→14). Tens: 13−7=6 (we borrowed 1→3→13). Hundreds: 1−1=0. Answer: ₹66.75.

skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.

choices.label: C. Profit = ₹178.75 − ₹245.50 = −₹66.75 (subtract the bigger from smaller... that gives a loss!)
choices.learning_concept: Profit = Selling Price MINUS Cost Price
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You subtracted in the wrong order! Profit = Selling Price − Cost Price = ₹245.50 − ₹178.75 = ₹66.75 (positive = profit!). If cost > selling price, THEN it's a loss. Here selling price (245.50) > cost (178.75), so it IS a profit of ₹66.75.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

choices.label: D. Profit = ₹245.50 + ₹178.75 = ₹424.25 (add them for total amount)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Adding gives the total of both amounts, not the profit! Profit is the DIFFERENCE between what you earn and what you spend: Profit = Selling Price − Cost Price = ₹245.50 − ₹178.75 = ₹66.75. In word problems, 'profit' and 'how much more' mean SUBTRACT.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

rounds.situation: It is the Grand Market Day — the biggest shopping event of the year! The Mayor is visiting, the newspaper is covering the market, and your shop is the featured 'Young Entrepreneur' booth. You must present your journey — from struggling with ₹12.50 change on Day 1 to managing profit percentages and audit-ready books. This is your moment to show the world what decimals can do!
rounds.goal: Apply ALL decimal concepts in one final showcase that demonstrates your complete mastery!
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: True mastery means connecting all concepts together — place value, comparing, adding, subtracting, multiplying, rounding, converting, percentages, and profit/loss. When you see how they all connect through decimals, mathematics becomes a powerful tool for understanding and running the world.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Looking back at all 14 days, which decimal skill surprised you the most? Which one will you use most in everyday life?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon grand market celebration with decorated stalls, Mayor cutting ribbon at featured young entrepreneur booth, newspaper cameras, crowd of impressed visitors, young shopkeeper proudly displaying charts and products, confetti and banners, Pixar-style

choices.label: A. The next number in 0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 1.1, ___ is 1.4 (pattern: add 0.3 each time)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Find the pattern by looking at differences: 0.5−0.2=0.3, 0.8−0.5=0.3, 1.1−0.8=0.3. The rule is 'add 0.3 each time.' So next: 1.1 + 0.3 = 1.4. Decimal patterns work just like whole number patterns — find the rule (add, subtract, multiply) and apply it!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.
skill_explanation.creativity: Not settling for the obvious solution builds creative problem-solving.

choices.label: B. The next number is 1.5 (I think the pattern adds 0.4, then 0.3, then 0.3...)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Check the differences carefully: 0.5−0.2=0.3, 0.8−0.5=0.3, 1.1−0.8=0.3. The pattern is consistent: always +0.3. So next = 1.1 + 0.3 = 1.4 (not 1.5). Always calculate ALL the differences to confirm the pattern is constant.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

choices.label: C. The next number is 1.3 (I added 0.2 because the sequence started with 0.2)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 The starting value (0.2) is not the same as the pattern rule. Find the rule by subtracting consecutive terms: 0.5−0.2=0.3. The pattern adds 0.3 each time, not 0.2. So: 1.1 + 0.3 = 1.4. Always find the pattern from the differences between terms!

skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

choices.label: D. The next number is 2.2 (double 1.1 since the pattern doubles)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 This is an ADDITIVE pattern (add the same amount), not multiplicative (doubling). Check: 0.5 is NOT double 0.2 (that would be 0.4). The constant difference is 0.3. So the sequence is: 0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 1.1, 1.4, 1.7, 2.0... Each term = previous + 0.3.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

glossary_terms.definition: A number that uses a decimal point to show a value between whole numbers. The decimal point separates the whole number part from the fractional part. For example, 12.75 means 12 whole and 75 hundredths.

The value of a digit based on its position in a number. In 12.75: 1 is in the tens place (value 10), 2 is in the ones place (value 2), 7 is in the tenths place (value 0.7), and 5 is in the hundredths place (value 0.05).
A number expressed as a fraction of 100. The symbol is %. For example, 25% means 25 out of 100, which equals 0.25 as a decimal or 1/4 as a fraction.

Replacing a number with a nearby simpler value. To round to one decimal place, look at the second decimal digit: if it is 5 or more, round up; if it is less than 5, round down. For example, 3.47 rounds to 3.5.
The money earned when selling price is more than cost price. Profit = Selling Price - Cost Price. Profit percentage = (Profit / Cost Price) × 100.
The money lost when selling price is less than cost price. Loss = Cost Price - Selling Price. Loss percentage = (Loss / Cost Price) × 100.
The first digit position after the decimal point. It represents parts out of 10. In 0.7, the 7 is in the tenths place, meaning seven-tenths or 7/10.
The second digit position after the decimal point. It represents parts out of 100. In 0.75, the 5 is in the hundredths place, meaning five-hundredths or 5/100.
Decimals that have the same value even though they look different. For example, 0.5 = 0.50 = 0.500. Adding trailing zeros after the last non-zero decimal digit does not change the value.

endings.title: Market Champion
endings.message: You are the undisputed Market Champion! Your decimal skills are extraordinary — every bill is perfect, every percentage is calculated instantly, and every customer trusts you completely. The Mayor presents you with the 'Young Entrepreneur of the Year' award, the newspaper features your shop on the front page, and other shopkeepers come to learn from you. You proved that decimals are not just numbers — they are the language of business!

endings.title: Popular Shop
endings.message: Your Decimal Market shop is the most popular in the bazaar! Customers line up because they know your bills are always accurate and your prices are fair. Your reputation is solid, your team works well, and your profit margins are healthy. You might not be a maths genius yet, but you are well on your way!

endings.title: Average Shop
endings.message: Your shop is doing okay — not great, not terrible. Some bills are correct, some have small decimal errors. Customers are satisfied but not amazed. Your skills improved over the 14 days, but there is still room for growth. The foundation is there — with more practice, you could become the market champion. Every expert was once a beginner!

endings.title: Struggling Shop
endings.message: Your shop is struggling. Too many billing errors crept into your calculations — wrong change, incorrect discounts, and misplaced decimal points. Customers lost trust and some stopped coming. The good news? You learned from every mistake. Decimals are tricky, but practice makes perfect. Do not give up — come back and try again!

endings.title: Shop Closed
endings.message: The shop had to close its doors. Wrong decimal calculations led to wrong bills, wrong bills led to lost trust, and lost trust meant no customers. But here is the truth — every successful shopkeeper failed before they succeeded. Decimals are the language of money, and money is the language of business. Come back, sharpen your skills, and try again. Your next attempt will be better!
